title: UX designer with a fully designed card game — what tools/options do I actually have to make a digital prototype that follows logic and multiplayer?
author: xcantene
selftext:
Hi everyone,

I’m a UX/Product designer (10+ years in SaaS and e-commerce) who has spent the last 3 years designing and balancing a competitive card game called **Skyland: Hunt Protocol**.

It’s not a classic 1v1 card battler. All players fight the same monster at the same time and race to kill it with the fewest scored cards. The core loop is about building efficient chains, managing stamina/ether, and deciding when to trash cards to fix your combo. I have 4 unique decks, 8 hunters with abilities, a permanent upgrade system, and the whole thing is already fully playable and balanced on Tabletopia.

The original plan was physical, but after doing all the printing/fulfillment math it looks almost impossible to make work financially. So I’m now seriously looking at digital options.

I know almost nothing about coding or game development. I’m good at UX/UI and I already have (or am paying artists for) all the real art assets, card designs, hunter illustrations, etc. I don’t want tools that force me to use only AI-generated art.

What I’m looking for is something that lets me focus on **building the actual mechanics and logics** (chains, combo resolution, trashing with cascade effects, continuing combos across turns, monster reactions, tracking stats, upgrade system, etc.) while I can use my own art assets instead of placeholders later. It is okay to start with placeholders, but I want to be able to put my own art and IP on it.

Are there any realistic tools or paths for someone in my position?  
Is this even doable without becoming a full developer and spending years learning the skill?  
Any guidance, tool recommendations, or “here’s what I would do” stories would be really helpful.

If you want to know more about the game these are the rules: [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1EFaNQ2yThOdNIbd9J8Lb7Kry75kV-DJi2MRxa8WJKBU/edit?usp=sharing](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1EFaNQ2yThOdNIbd9J8Lb7Kry75kV-DJi2MRxa8WJKBU/edit?usp=sharing)

Thanks in advance!

comments.author: Melodic-Chemistry127
comments.body:
What happens in a situation where a hunter would reduce the monster to low hp and decides not to play instead. How do you resolve a situation where no one wants to act because they would set up the next player in the turn order for victory?

At this point, if you want to turn this into an actual product, the AI is not there yet to allow you to autopilot this. Especially because multiplayer adds tons of complexity. You will also want a certain level of polish if you want people to be regularly returning to this.

You could try paying for Codex and whipping it out in Godot(C#) or Unity and proving me wrong, but I don't think it's going to happen. You would need to understand how to design software first or you're going to hit one wall after another.

replies.author: xcantene
replies.body:
Yeah, that is what I thought. I do not think there is the tech yet for this, unless I pay for development to create all raw coding. 

About your question on the game. I am not fully sure if I got the question right.   
But pretty much whoever makes the monster reach 0 health sets the combo to beat and 1 last turn for all other players. So lets say that combo is 4 cards, others must defeat it in 4 cards or fewer. If there is a tie on 4 cards, whoever got fewer monster hints is the winner; if that is still a tie, no one claims the monster.

Now, what I am thinking you are asking is an exploit, lets say you know you can finish the monster in 3 counted cards, and you intentionally force others to finish first. There is no pass action, but maybe you just keep discarding and drawing cards. In this case, it would be the same rule above, but if you run out of cards in your deck, you are out of the hunt. So it could be a good mind game that so far I have not seen anyone play it out on the playtests I have run so I may try it myself 😃

replies.author: Melodic-Chemistry127
replies.body:
Maybe I misunderstood your design doc, but I was assuming that the monster has shared HP for everyone. E.g. if the monster has 100 hp, player A hits it for 20 hp, then the remaining players only need to reduce it by 80 hp to kill it. If that's the case, people will try to avoid attacking if they'd know they're going to put the monster in the kill range for someone else. If each player has their own instance of the monster, then it's not an issue.

By the way, I don't think the implementation is as easy as the other commenter is insinuating. I've been a software dev for over 20 years and multiplayer adds a whole bunch of complexity to otherwise relatively simple concept. I'm also assuming you want a certain level of audio visual polish, because you want players to be coming back.

I strongly suggest you either get a programmer on board, or pay someone if that's viable for you. Fumbling multiplayer is too easy and AI won't save you if you don't know what you're doing.

replies.author: xcantene
replies.body:
yup. so pretty much everyone fights the same monsters but on their own terms. That is why is more of a PvE because your target is the monster. But also, you gotta try to finish it quickly before others do.  
  
Thank you a lot for the comments and help! I am really feeling that maybe this is not the time yet for me to get into digital and should focus still on my print method for now, even if it will be super hard to deliver and then take care of shipments and other factors that I would love to avoid.

replies.author: Melodic-Chemistry127
replies.body:
Generally, if you're building an actual commercial product, think of multiplayer as adding 3-5x complexity on top of what you're actually building. You will need to handle server infrastructure, some sort of database, concurrency, server authority, synchronization and a bunch of other stuff. In the off chance your game blows up, you would also need to handle scaling while keeping the hosting costs reasonable. That's a level of complexity AI will definitely screw up if you can't wrangle it properly.

I love your card design, by the way. If you'll need some advice later down the line, don't hesitate to send a DM. I would absolutely love to see this game on Steam one day.

comments.author: Unturned1
comments.body: Nothing exists which will do this for you. You should just take a game engine and implement it yourself. Look up how to use claude code or codex along with an MCP-server. Card games are 90% UI anyways which is your strength. The amount of code needed is relatively low, and unless I am missing something your aren't going to have crazy design requirements.

replies.author: xcantene
replies.body:
How about paying someone for it? Because honestly, I already have a lot on my plate to dump more time on learning new skills, downloading software, and putting in more new effort. 

I honestly do not know how hard it would be to code the logic on the chains for the game, since this is not a duel game where you play a card, lower health to the other player, and keep drawing.

replies.author: Unturned1
replies.body:
After reading the rules I don't see anything super hard about the game logic, inevitably there will be a ton of edge cases that you as the designer will need to resolve to give guidance of how the code should behave. Finding someone to do this is possible in my opinion there are firms which specialize in doing this kind of contract work. If you just need a prototype maybe even one person could do it quickly. 

The biggest question is why do you want to do this? If you want to produce a game to make money this approach is dubious because what exactly is your value proposition other than you came up with a card game with some rules and maybe theming. 

If you do not want to do it to make money and this is hobby then you could probably spend some cash to get the thing you want to personally play and enjoy alone.

If you want to build games as hobby and want video game versions you should learn to build video games, because nobody is going to do it exactly how you want on a budget...

You should probably answer this question for yourself first before you decide.

replies.author: xcantene
replies.body:
Well, the main goal is to eventually build my own small game studio.

Physical was the first path because it’s what I can fully control and deliver with my current skills (UX + project management + artists). Digital is the long-term plan, so I can start releasing games and grow the studio step by step.

Regarding value proposition, I’m trying to create something genuinely different from the usual 1v1 dueling card games. This is a **multiplayer efficiency race** where everyone fights the same monster at the same time. The skill comes from building the most elegant, low-scored combo while managing resources and surviving retaliation. It’s closer to a puzzle-solving race than a traditional card battler. That’s the new experience I’m going for.

I understand it’s still early, which is why I’m here asking for realistic advice before I invest more.

comments.author: ilrein91
comments.body: You have a few options on the table, you can use Godot or phaserjs with Claude or Codex and you can probably build the entire thing. Feel free to dm me.

comments.author: HealthyWest6482
comments.body:
From my experience - Codex/Claude are both very smart, but very naive when it comes to making anything interesting/fun mechanically. You'll probably have to brainstorm some genuinely cool shit - probably better results throwing the table at the wall with 'Chat' versions rather than agents and don't let them get sycophantic on your ass because they will glaze you like a donut on every push.

But seeing as you already have the rules documented out, you're like 80% there. Codex/Claude would both do well at implementing systems of logic. You could probably pass your rule documentation into GPT 5.5 or Claude Chat -> ask them to spit out a module friendly MD of each feature -> create a spec that pieces all of it together in architecture -> throw the architecture + module pieces at Opus or Codex for work.
